analysis.one_liner: Requires large warehouse employers to disclose and limit work quotas, grant paid rest breaks, and set injury safety standards.
analysis.headline: Introduced with support from 12 senators including two Republicans, but the Senate labor committee has taken no action on it since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets large warehouse and distribution employers (those with more than 200 workers at covered facilities) that use productivity quotas. It would require employers to tell workers in writing about every quota, the surveillance technology used to track them, and any discipline that can follow a miss; bar quotas that measure output in stretches shorter than a day, count bathroom breaks against output, or block legally required breaks and accommodations; guarantee a paid 15-minute rest break every 4 hours; let workers see, correct, and supplement the speed data collected on them; and penalize retaliation. It also directs OSHA to write new standards on warehouse ergonomics and on prompt medical referral for injuries, adds a National Labor Relations Act rule against quotas that discourage union rights, makes the FTC a second enforcer, and bans forced arbitration for claims under the act.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and distribution workers subject to productivity quotas — pickers, packers, loaders, and order-fillers at large facilities, including temps and contractors — gain enforceable rights to know their quotas, take paid breaks, access the speed data used against them, and challenge retaliation in court rather than forced arbitration. Labor organizations and worker advocacy groups gain a formal role in inspections, complaint filings, and enforcement training.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give each covered worker a written description of every quota, including the target, how it is calculated, the surveillance technology used to monitor it, any third parties the data goes to, and the discipline a miss can trigger — with updates at least two business days before changes take effect.

Quotas may not measure output over intervals shorter than a day, may not count paid breaks or bathroom time (including travel to and from a restroom) against output, and may not prevent legally required meal or rest periods, safety compliance, or accommodations; discipline for missing a quota that violates these rules, was never disclosed, is based purely on ranking against coworkers, or rests on continuously tallying off-task time is barred.

Workers get a paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked, must be told about it in their primary language at hiring, and retaliation for taking or requesting breaks is prohibited, with a rebuttable presumption of retaliation if an adverse action follows protected activity within 90 days.

Workers (or a designated union or advocate representative) can request copies of their work speed data and aggregated data for coworkers in readable form, supplement the record with explanations for off-task time, and have inaccurate data corrected — with any discipline based on the bad data reviewed and adjusted.

The Labor Department must open an on-site investigation of any covered employer whose injury rate is at least 1.5 times the warehousing industry average with 40,000+ annual work hours, or that draws at least 5 credible complaints at a worksite in a year, and civil penalties reach up to $76,987 per violation and $769,870 for repeat or willful violations; forced arbitration agreements and class-action waivers are unenforceable for these claims, and workers can sue for damages including $10,000-$25,000 per violation.

OSHA must issue standards within fixed deadlines requiring ergonomic hazard evaluation and control, medical management, onsite first aiders who promptly refer injured workers for treatment, and board-certified occupational medicine consultation; employers must fix serious, willful, or repeated violations on schedule even while contesting them, unless they win a stay.

Imposing a quota that significantly discourages union activity becomes an unfair labor practice, with a rebuttable presumption of retaliation for quotas imposed within 90 days of protected organizing.

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse, fulfillment, wholesale, and express delivery employers — including staffing agencies and contractors — bear the compliance costs: written quota disclosures and training, rest breaks paid at the regular rate, recordkeeping and data-access systems, legal exposure to lawsuits and new civil penalties, and re-engineered workflows to meet the OSHA ergonomic and medical-referral standards. Some of these costs would likely reach consumers through higher prices or slower delivery. Companies that do not monitor work speed data are explicitly exempt from the recordkeeping and data-provision duties.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on large employers — paid breaks, disclosure and recordkeeping systems, penalty exposure, and new OSHA-mandated ergonomics and medical programs — some portion of which would likely be passed to consumers through higher prices or slower, costlier delivery; the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in federal appropriations for 2026-2036 to administer it.

The bill does not ban quotas; a compliant quota is still lawful, and an employer that never monitors work speed data owes no recordkeeping or data-access duties, so the practical protections depend heavily on how the Labor Department and the new Fairness and Transparency Office write rules and enforce them.

The strongest good-faith objection is that quotas and speed data are what make same-day and low-cost fulfillment possible, and the bill's near-ban on sub-daily output measurement, limits on using ranking or off-task-time data in discipline, and removal of forced arbitration would substantially rework how the sector manages performance — costs defenders argue ultimately land on workers through reduced flexibility and on consumers.
The bill reaches only employers with more than 200 employees at covered facilities (counting affiliates), leaving smaller warehouses and distribution operations unaffected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly targeted population of quota-bound warehouse workers, the bill delivers concrete, enforceable rights — knowing the quota, paid breaks, access to the data used to discipline them, court access instead of arbitration — at a real but concentrated cost to a handful of very large logistics employers. The OSHA ergonomics standard responds to documented high injury rates in warehousing. The main honest concerns are enforcement quality (the bill relies on a new office and regulatory machinery to work), compliance costs that may partly reach consumers, and the exclusion of smaller employers. The design does not appear to entrench any industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 31, 2025, read twice, and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has held no markup or vote on it; Congress is still in session, so the bill remains alive but untouched.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced S. 2613, the Warehouse Worker Protection Act, in the Senate on July 31, 2025, joined on introduction day by Sens. Hawley and Marshall (Republicans), Sanders (Independent), and Padilla, Blumenthal, Welch, Warren, Murphy, and Smith (Democrats).

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the full action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote.
The bill has 12 cosponsors: 9 of 45 Senate Democrats, 2 of 55 Senate Republicans, and 1 of 2 Senate Independents.
If it were to move, the path runs through the HELP committee before any Senate floor consideration; the bill as written would also need companion House action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything: large warehouse and fulfillment operators face no new quota, break, or safety obligations, and warehouse workers' conditions are unchanged while the bill sits without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: The 12 cosponsors span parties — 9 of 45 Senate Democrats, 2 of 55 Senate Republicans (Hawley and Marshall), and 1 of 2 Independents (Sanders) — but the committee chair who controls its fate is a Republican, and no votes have occurred to measure the split.

industries.industry: Large warehouse and fulfillment operators (e-commerce retail logistics, third-party warehousing)
industries.note: These employers — the bill covers warehousing, wholesale, electronic shopping, and express delivery facilities with 200+ workers including affiliates — would face mandatory quota disclosure, a paid 15-minute break every 4 hours, data-access and recordkeeping duties, new OSHA ergonomics and medical-referral standards, penalty exposure up to $769,870 per willful violation, and no forced arbitration. Their interest in continuing quota-driven, lightly regulated operations runs against the workers' interest in enforceable limits.

industries.industry: Warehouse staffing agencies, contractors, and employee leasing firms
industries.note: The bill expressly brings temp firms, staffing agencies, and independent-contractor arrangements within the definition of covered employer, closing the common channel through which warehouse operators shift quota pressure onto non-employee labor.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and workforce productivity-data vendors
industries.note: The bill limits data collection to what is strictly necessary to monitor quota compliance, restricts disclosure, requires identifying third-party vendors to workers, and lets workers review and correct the data — narrowing the market for always-on employee monitoring in warehouses.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the HELP committee with no hearing or markup scheduled and 12 cosponsors — modest support for a Senate bill. Most referred bills never reach a committee vote, and the odds of floor action in this Congress look low unless warehouse conditions or organizing pressure elevate it; even if it cleared committee, it would need a House companion and floor votes in both chambers.
